# Review and fix a Drever deck

Commands below use npm's project-local runner. In a pnpm, Yarn, or Bun project, use `pnpm exec drever`, `yarn exec drever`, or `bunx --no-install drever` and the matching script runner instead.

Respect the requested scope. Report findings without editing for review-only requests; apply and verify fixes when asked to fix or polish.

This skill is the single owner of Drever's exhaustive rendered completion gate. Run it only after
the requested authoring or design pass is stable; creation, authoring, and design workflows use
source-only and affected-route checks while iterating. Every context report, check, browser
inspection, build, and export is valid only for the exact source, configuration, and assets that
existed when it ran. Any later mutation invalidates the affected evidence. If feedback arrives or a
file changes while review is running, cancel the affected work when possible or ignore its result,
apply the change first, and restart the affected review from fresh context. Never cite stale
evidence; evidence captured before the last relevant edit is stale.

1. When Drever MCP tools are available, start with `drever_get_current` and `drever_get_context`; use `drever_get_slide` for each affected source slice. Otherwise use `npm exec -- drever current --json` and `npm exec -- drever context --json`. Inspect the complete design contract, source map, and exact Step topology. When `drever.plan.json` exists, compare every planned narrative job, evidence requirement, focal artifact, composition recipe, density, and motion owner with the authored and rendered result; flag silent drift rather than judging the deck as an unrelated artifact.
2. Run `npm exec -- drever check --rendered --json` and inspect every source and rendered finding even when the command exits nonzero. Require the current report V2 and its `rendered` receipt; inspect the receipt and ruleset versions, engine, optional browser version, state count, status, and reason instead of inferring capture from diagnostic prose. A stored V1 report is source-only and cannot satisfy the rendered gate. Treat clipping, canvas overflow, text overlap, direct scroll overflow, and resolved solid-color contrast failures as blocking machine evidence. Investigate geometry, density, and indeterminate-paint warnings in the live deck; they are stable review leads, not aesthetic verdicts. Use `drever_check` as the faster source-only companion when MCP is connected, not as a replacement for rendered preflight.
3. Inspect every slide at Step 0 and every exact sparse Step state at the configured canvas size. Machine evidence narrows the search but does not judge hierarchy, beauty, motion meaning, contrast on complex paint, or intermediate frames. Use screenshots and audience judgment rather than judging source or a clean report alone. If rendered inspection cannot be obtained, report the missing evidence as a blocker and do not call the deck presentation-ready.
4. Prefer a connected Chrome DevTools MCP server for the final rendered gate. Probe it once with `list_pages`, open or navigate to the project-local preview in an isolated context, and use `emulate` or `resize_page` to match the configured canvas. Before judging a route, use `evaluate_script` to await `document.fonts.ready` and two animation frames. For every exact route, take a fresh `take_snapshot` for structure and then a `take_screenshot` for appearance; use evaluated computed styles, bounding boxes, client and scroll dimensions, and current animations to investigate clipping, overflow, typography, and continuity. Exercise adjacent states in both directions with real keyboard or pointer input. At the end, inspect preserved `list_console_messages` and `list_network_requests` for runtime, font, and asset failures. Screenshots and audience judgment—not snapshots, metrics, Lighthouse, or passing commands—decide visual readiness, and Chromium evidence alone does not prove another browser. If Chrome DevTools MCP is unavailable, use another connected browser surface that provides real screenshots and interaction; if no rendered evidence is possible, keep the blocker from step 3.
5. In a Drever development preview, run the version-matched `globalThis.__dreverExperimentalTextLayout()` probe through browser evaluation after fonts and paint settle. It uses Pretext to compare predicted and rendered line layout for supported visible plain-text blocks. Treat its report as advisory: inspect every finding in the actual DOM and screenshot, and do not infer a pass from an empty report. The probe deliberately skips rich inline markup, generated content, non-default wrapping or indentation, automatic hyphenation, columns, transforms, generic system fonts, and non-default word spacing or font shaping settings. Never auto-shrink copy or replace browser layout from this evidence.
6. Inspect `/document` for reading order and fully revealed content. Inspect both `/speaker` previews for notes, synchronization, and presentation usability. Exercise exact audience routes and every applicable built, reduced-motion, document, speaker, and export state. For public or shared decks, verify that the closing next action uses visible canonical absolute links and remains useful in rendered audience, document, and export output.
7. Test direct route loading in the live preview when delivery is in scope. Do not run a production
   build or export here; the delivery skill owns those artifacts after this rendered evidence is
   fresh.

Treat review as an iterative completion gate, not a final glance. A clean check and successful build prove structural validity, not narrative, visual, or interaction quality. Work through these passes:

When this is the completion gate after creation or a material edit, begin from the actual complete
first render as a fresh audience member. Do not rationalize a weak result from author intent.
Preserve successful claims, signature moments, routes, Steps, and design decisions while fixing
evidence-backed material issues. The goal is a better deck, not a visibly different second version;
leave sound choices untouched and never manufacture novelty or decoration to prove that review
happened.

1. **Narrative reasonableness:** Read the deck as an audience member. Verify that every slide advances the argument, relates concretely to the subject, supports its claim with useful evidence, and avoids abstract slogans, obvious filler, unexplained labels, and unnecessary density.
2. **Static visual quality:** Start with a blocking readability scan, then inspect every rendered state at the configured canvas size. Every visible authored string is a reading promise. Treat any heading, body copy, label, caption, legend, annotation, link, code, table cell, or control that is not immediately legible at presentation distance on the configured canvas as a blocking P0 defect. If text is not meant to be read, use a non-text visual texture instead of fake microcopy. Inspect each rendered descendant's computed font size, weight, line height, margin, padding, gap, and foreground against the worst background, Step state, and motion frame; declared CSS and a passing contrast ratio are not proof, and an ancestor's `color` is not proof. Check that scoped local CSS actually normalizes conflicting Theme-owned Markdown margins, maximum widths, line height, text transform, and foreground without globally resetting the deck. Dim background layers or decoration, never a container that also contains required text. Keep every label and copy block fully contained within the shape or surface that visually owns it, with deliberate padding in every Step and intermediate frame. For circles, rings, clipped polygons, and other non-rectangular owners, validate the usable inner silhouette after borders and padding, not merely the rectangular bounding box. If the copy cannot fit, enlarge or reflow the owner, or move the label outside with an explicit association. Never repair it by clipping, overlap, or shrinking below presentation legibility. Non-overlap is only a baseline: verify that every status, label, and annotation has a clear spatial owner and intentional reading-order relationship instead of merely occupying a free patch of canvas. Confirm that every line or connector ends exactly at its intended node center, edge, or port and stays centered on its route; flag unexplained overshoot even when nothing clips. Then check hierarchy, alignment, spacing, type, backgrounds, recurring motifs, link and control affordances, composition rhythm across the deck, and the largest painted footprint. The claim or audience outcome should own the strongest emphasis; viewport dimensions, API signatures, filenames, and other implementation literals remain supporting evidence unless the literal is the claim. Backgrounds remain subordinate unless they are the evidence. Apply a first-glance test: if a grid, topology, particle, glow, ambient motion, or implementation label wins attention before the title or evidence, reduce it and strengthen the foreground surface separation. Repeated elements remain intentionally consistent.
3. **Motion and continuity:** Inspect the initial state, intermediate frames, settled state, and reverse handoff for every transition and Step change. Treat Step as a real DOM wrapper: verify that its positioned bounds and the containing block of every absolute descendant remain invariant in pending, active, and complete states, with no top-of-slide or cross-container rebase when `transform` or individual `translate` changes. Require exactly one motion owner per spatial payload—a Step reveal, navigation continuity, or local live-DOM/keyframe cue—and one clear focal object with a narrative reason. Confirm authored keyframes begin only while the slide is active and, for Step-owned cues, while that Step is active; inactive mounted slides must not consume them early. Flag flashes, jitter, ghosting, stretched text or rules, abrupt shadow or filter changes, clipped paint, premature timing, and movement that competes with the claim.
4. **Interaction and surfaces:** Use the deck rather than only looking at it. Verify navigation, hover, focus, keyboard behavior, toolbar and focus tools, exact routes, reload, history, speaker synchronization, `/speaker`, `/document`, reduced motion, and export-relevant states. Controls outside the slide remain stable and usable while slide content moves.
5. **Technical and accessibility:** Check console output, fonts, assets, rendered names, roles, states, tab order, keyboard operation, visible focus, contrast, alternatives, captions, reading order, deterministic media, and relevant tests. At every Step state, confirm that accessible names and descriptions reveal only the information currently available visually; a persistent label must not summarize a pending Step outcome. Confirm that live behavior has an understandable static or reduced-motion result.

For every prominent sentence, object, animation, background treatment, and control, ask what job it performs. Simplify or remove it when the answer does not serve the claim, audience, or operation of the deck. Fix the highest-severity causes, refresh the live render, and repeat the affected passes and adjacent handoffs until no material defect remains. If an external blocker or genuine user judgment remains, state it explicitly; never call a deck ready because its source looked plausible or a command succeeded.

Review for:

- A coherent story, one dominant idea per slide, useful evidence, and a clear conclusion. Motion must not disguise abstract slogans or missing reasoning.
- Language that matches the user's brief unless another language was explicitly chosen, with terminology and punctuation consistent across visible copy, notes, and labels.
- A flagship product tour that demonstrates its central promise through one concrete audience decision and a traceable artifact lifecycle instead of presenting a feature catalog. Require the real interaction and outcome to occur in the deck; move secondary inventory to focused examples.
- Stable alignment, deliberate spacing, immediately legible essential text, sufficient contrast on the worst rendered surface and Step state, and no clipping or overflow.
- Display headings whose line breaks preserve short clauses and verb phrases before visual rhythm, with no stranded conjunction, governing verb, or opening word of a new clause at the configured canvas or responsive widths.
- A subject-led visual premise with a few memorable signature moments and quieter supporting slides. Flag a deck made almost entirely from interchangeable text cards, generic gradients, or preset surfaces even when each individual slide is tidy.
- A defensible ceiling after correctness: ask what one scene the audience will remember and why it could not belong to an unrelated topic. If there is no answer, redesign exactly one high-value beat around a topic-specific artifact and meaningful transformation; do not decorate or regenerate the whole deck.
- Composition that follows the content instead of repeating one convenient template. Flag a deck whose slides mostly use the same left-copy/right-artifact split when centered statements, full-canvas diagrams, single artifacts, sequences, comparisons, data fields, or asymmetric editorial layouts would explain individual ideas more clearly. Do not demand visual variety without a narrative reason.
- In a catalog or family of reference decks, each design system must have a distinct structural identity. Flag recolored versions of the same short narrative, page count, two-column silhouette, persistent artifact, or transition sequence; compare their density, composition rhythm, Step grammar, transition cadence, and signature moments rather than palette alone.
- When a slide pairs a prose-heavy narrative region with supporting content, flag another prose-heavy panel when the support could communicate through a diagram, artifact, media frame, data mark, spatial form, or quiet subject-led abstraction. Keep its text to functional labels or captions unless comparing the texts is the claim.
- Code examples that use an explicit language and produce visibly distinct, contrast-safe syntax tokens. Flag a centerpiece example rendered as undifferentiated monochrome source or a hand-built `<pre>` that bypasses the configured highlighter.
- Step changes that reveal meaning without moving persistent content.
- Motion that has a clear narrative job, follows the content flow, fits the theme, uses quiet contextual delight sparingly, avoids repeated generic entrances, and respects reduced motion.
- A coherent theme-led transition vocabulary rather than one mandatory effect. Flag both random effects and a View Transition applied to every edge without narrative need. Direct cuts, quiet fades, local live-DOM handoffs, Steps, and a few continuity transitions may coexist when their cadence and gesture fit the subject; a traditional or minimal deck may use mostly cuts.
- One primary motion per moment across native transitions, Steps, kinetic type, video, 3D, and third-party animation, with at most one quieter supporting cue in the same causal chain. Multiple techniques must serialize around one focal object instead of competing simultaneously. If a headline or core object changes, Stage decoration and neighboring cards stay still; recurring decoration does not earn motion merely by recurring. Ask: What single object should the audience follow? If the answer names two, remove or sequence one.
- Key objects whose full narrative lifecycle is coherent: they may begin completely off-stage, enter as evidence, dock at low contrast when they become context, and retire when they stop supporting the claim. Prefer a short connected sequence when one concrete artifact can take a distinct narrative role on each adjacent slide while the surrounding context or surface changes. Flag a visible fragment that communicates nothing, a disconnected entrance, repeated composition without a new job, or continued motion that no longer carries meaning.
- Continuity sequences that end when their object stops carrying the argument. Flag a persistent artifact placed beside new copy on every slide only because a shared transition is available; prefer a new composition, direct cut, or narrowly declared local `SlideTransition` for the edge where the story changes canvases.
- Timing that lets the audience perceive any required initial state and chooses delay and duration from reading and narrative causality instead of a fixed rule. Quiet cues must remain perceptible at presentation distance.
- Cues that animate only properties carrying the semantic change. Flag an unrelated type recolor, accent movement, or Stage shift added to intensify an already clear effect.
- Presenter-driven reveals modeled as Steps instead of inline buttons. Keep a direct control only when manipulating it is itself the lesson.
- Stage backgrounds, page information, persistent titles, audience controls, dialogs, and foreground chrome that remain stationary across slide transitions; animate only the smallest changed sub-element. Flag any full-canvas background placed in a continuity group because its extracted snapshot can paint above the slide content.
- Full-canvas scenes with one stable positioned slide-relative root and explicit bounds. Their outer scene contains paint at the canvas edge while inner cards, media, shadows, glows, filters, and transformed intermediate frames retain the space they require; flag both browser-surface spill and hard-clipped required paint.
- Recurring motifs whose position, thickness, opacity, paint, orientation, and cross-axis alignment remain invariant across adjacent slides unless a meaningful chapter, comparison, or state change clearly explains and sustains the move; lines and bands should translate along their logical axis or reveal through an inner mask instead of stretching.
- Cards, panels, and media frames whose required shadows, glows, outlines, and filters are never hard-clipped; shadow endpoints must use matching lists with transparent colors instead of `none`.
- Continuity boundaries that carry either the same object or two adjacent objects with an immediately legible semantic or visual correspondence. Matching color or shape alone is insufficient: require one stable shared feature, identical explicit endpoint inline size, block size, aspect ratio, and `box-sizing`, plus deliberate paint, text metrics, wrapping, and media crop. Parent layout may reposition the fixed shell; the captured shell itself must not change shape. Charge the handoff to the moment's primary motion budget. Flag arbitrary morphs, grow-then-shrink settling, and ghosting as snapshot-geometry mismatches before changing timing or easing.
- Related copy effects that run locally after capture in one fixed slot with stable type metrics and accessible final text; changing glyphs must not share a View Transition, scale, or crossfade, and reduced motion must expose the final copy immediately.
- Moving indicators with one legible role: a cursor or focus reticle has a recognizable hotspot that lands exactly on a meaningful target, and a text caret shares the inline wrapper of the word it follows instead of floating relative to the panel. A route signal stays centered on its path and reaches the authored endpoint. Marker and milestones share one local positioned coordinate system with border-box geometry; flag magic-pixel travel measured from another container.
- External motion or spatial tools that supply a justified capability rather than a borrowed showcase style. Require a focused working example instead of a library name or link, plus current official documentation and license review before copied code or assets. Prefer native or small local React for simple effects; consult the [non-exhaustive Motion references](https://drever.dev/docs/motion/#external-tools) only when useful.
- Live integrations with accessible final semantics, keyboard behavior, deterministic loading and export readiness, reduced-motion output, and a stable poster or authored fallback where live document or export rendering is inappropriate. A loop is valid only when ongoing change is the subject; it must be deterministic, begin its first meaningful update on active audience entry, pause outside that surface, and have an intentional static endpoint. Animated numbers, labels, and charts share one frame and stable numeric geometry without frame-by-frame announcements.
- Charts whose form answers the claim: bars compare, dots rank, lines show a path, areas emphasize magnitude over a path, and donuts show a bounded part of a whole. Flag redundant series, ornamental smoothing, 3D, legends, labels, or interaction, and require the same data to produce a complete accessible description plus deterministic document and export output.
- Audio-reactive integrations that use one clear audience permission gesture by default, explain that microphone-backed analysis hears nearby sound or music played through speakers rather than headphones, keep capture local, stop every permissioned track and animation frame on deactivation, settle to an authored still state on silence, and remain static and permission-free elsewhere. Accept an automatic request only when immediate microphone response is the active opening slide's premise, visible copy explains why it appears, denial remains discoverable, and inactive slides, previews, Speaker View, Document View, and export never prompt. Treat `RoomAudio` as an incubating workspace reference rather than a published authoring API, treat `Soundtrack` as a separate playback contract, and verify the final media response is CORS-readable before accepting any remote stream as genuinely frequency-reactive.
- Animated and spatial components sized for their largest transformed and painted footprint across the whole sequence. At maximum expansion, 2D or 3D layers retain clear space from tracks, labels, and adjacent copy; hiding overflow is not a valid repair.
- Card walls and breadth montages with terse labels, one collective claim, and a deterministic non-linear reveal order. Flag runtime-random placement or timing, competing card-level headlines, unstable endpoints, and incomplete reduced-motion or export states.
- Bespoke CSS, SVG, canvas, or React judged by its explanatory and atmospheric value rather than its line count. Long local visual code is acceptable when ownership is clear, states are deterministic, and the rendered result earns it; remove only weak, redundant, or unmaintainable work.
- Correct headings, alternatives, captions, focus behavior, and document reading order.
- Working exact deep links, reload, history, speaker synchronization, build output, and export readiness.

For motion defects, inspect intermediate frames and the finished handoff in both directions, not only the endpoints. Verify that repeated Step changes do not move persistent text and that toolbar hover and focus remain live. Compare `getBoundingClientRect()` and computed styles before, during, and after activation: an absolute child must retain the same containing geometry, and every required painted footprint must remain within its authored surface and the canvas. For continuity defects, compare endpoint width, height, and aspect ratio plus computed paint styles. Prefer a fixed shared shell, invariant shrink-wrapped text, or explicit media fitting. A fixed width alone is insufficient when height or aspect ratio changes. Keep changing copy outside the shared bitmap. If kinetic type is intentional, require a local animation after capture, an identical fixed slot, stable font metrics, and non-overlapping exit and reveal phases; a shared transition, crossfade, or scaled glyph handoff is a defect. Absolute positioning is useful only when it produces equivalent containing geometry at both endpoints.

If an intermittent flash remains despite invariant endpoints, inspect high-frequency intermediate frames for a briefly exposed root or continuity capture. When the live DOM should own that exact adjacent handoff, use `SlideTransition` to bypass native capture before it starts and gate the local animation to the active slide plus the runtime local-transition marker. Calling `skipTransition()` after capture is not a repair because the faulty bitmap may already have been presented.

When Stage modules are configured, verify that the audience reuses the same background and foreground instances while position props update, page information does not change on a Step-only navigation, and no full Stage layer joins the slide transition. Check both speaker previews plus every document and export page; Stage effects must respect `renderMode`, reduced motion, repeated IDs, and export readiness. Nested Stage components may read state with `useStage()`.

Fix the cause in authored MDX, configuration, local components, or styles. Do not patch generated output or add legacy-browser fallbacks.

After the last relevant source mutation, rerun `npm exec -- drever context --json`,
`npm exec -- drever check --rendered --json`, affected browser states, and relevant project tests.
Reinspect the whole deck after changing a shared theme, layout, Stage layer, or component; otherwise
reinspect affected states and adjacent handoffs. Do not run the production build here. Source review
and successful commands do not count as the Draft 1 rendered refinement. Report findings by
severity with the slide, Step, source location, applied fix, and final evidence, and state that the
evidence follows the final relevant edit.
